prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "TORONTO DOMINION BANK" (ticker TD). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:

   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)

   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: TD is one of Canada's two top-dog banks and its shares have strong momentum (+49% over 52 weeks), but it is not a leader in an emerging industry, has no Rule Breaker innovation and is still repairing damage from its 2024 US anti-money-laundering guilty plea, so it fits Gardner's Rule Breaker approach poorly.
summaries.buffett: TD has the durable, understandable franchise Buffett likes in banks, with sticky low-cost deposits in a five-bank Canadian oligopoly and dividends paid every year since 1857. Against that, its US AML failures showed weak controls, it is highly leveraged like all banks, and at about 18x trailing earnings and 2.1x book it offers little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value TD's oligopoly position and long record, but inverting would highlight what went wrong: years of US AML control failures led to US$3.088B of penalties and an asset cap, a reminder that incentives and culture can fail inside a big bank; it is a recovering franchise, not an obvious bargain.
summaries.lynch: TD is a stalwart in recovery: adjusted EPS fell to C$7.81 in FY2024 after the AML penalties and is expected to rise about 21% to C$10.12 in FY2026. At about 17x forward earnings with a 2.6% dividend yield, the PEG is under 1 on this rebound, but the growth is a one-off recovery rather than lasting fast growth.
summaries.fisher: TD has deep management bench strength and strong sales in Canadian retail, cards and direct investing, but Fisher's points on management integrity and controls are weakened by the US AML failures, and banking offers limited room for new products to drive outsized growth.
summaries.graham: TD passes Graham's tests for size, a long profit record and an unbroken dividend since 1857, and EPS rose from C$4.21 in FY2015 to C$11.56 in FY2025, but it fails on price: a trailing P/E of about 18 and price-to-book of about 2.1 give P/E x P/B near 39, well above Graham's 22.5 limit.
summaries.thiel: TD does not fit Thiel's Zero to One model: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and competes in a mature, regulated oligopoly rather than a new market it created.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner favours efficient growers riding big platform shifts; TD is cutting costs (C$2-2.5B of targeted annualized savings, fewer management layers) and talks of scaling AI, but it is a mature bank in a turnaround, not a prime beneficiary of a technology shift.
summaries.druckenmiller: TD's improving earnings (Q3 2026 adjusted EPS C$2.77 vs C$2.20 a year earlier, beating the C$2.47 consensus) and large buybacks fit Druckenmiller's focus on change at the margin, but bank stocks are sensitive to rates, credit, the Canadian economy and US tariffs, and the US asset cap limits upside.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith generally avoids banks because of leverage and dependence on outside factors, so TD, whose ROE was 15.8% in Q3 2026 only with liabilities about 15.6x equity, falls outside his good-company criteria.
summaries.greenblatt: The Magic Formula excludes financial firms like banks, so TD's return on capital and earnings yield (about 5.5%) cannot be measured on Greenblatt's terms and it is not a fit.
summaries.akre: TD has a good core Canadian business, but Akre's management leg is weakened by the US AML failures and a new CEO since February 2025, and its reinvestment leg is limited by bank capital rules and the US$434B asset cap on its US bank.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai looks for simple businesses at deep discounts during temporary trouble; TD's AML crisis was such a fixable setback, but after a 49% rise over 52 weeks the shares trade near their 52-week high at about 2.1x book, so the bargain has largely gone.
summaries.wood: TD is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's sense; it is an incumbent that fintech and digital banking challengers target, so it does not fit Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: TD matches Ackman's taste for simple, dominant businesses with high barriers to entry, and its turnaround with a C$8B FY2026 buyback is the kind of catalyst he likes, but leverage, rate and credit exposure and US regulatory constraints weaken the fit.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared model is barely visible at TD: its scale lowers costs, but it keeps the savings as margins rather than passing them back to customers the way Costco or Amazon do.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge emerging markets; a bank with roots back to 1855 in a mature market is far from Sequoia's style.
summaries.nash: TD passes Nash's screens on scale, profitability and a 0.76% short interest, but fails several hard ones: underlying revenue growth is below 10%, bank leverage fails the banker's-lending test, free cash flow is not meaningful and it faces ongoing AML regulatory threats, scoring about 60 of 130 on his 13 categories.

momentum.evidence: TD's NYSE shares rose 49.1% over the 52 weeks to mid-October 2026, to US$120.39 on October 16 from a 52-week low of US$78.43, well ahead of the broad market.

g4.evidence: CEO Raymond Chun, a TD veteran since 1992, has delivered a credible turnaround since February 2025, but TD is a widely held bank (about 57% institutional ownership) with no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: After its rally the stock trades above the US$115.4 average analyst target (14 analysts, consensus Buy), so some analysts see it as fully valued, though it is not commonly called overvalued.

simple.evidence: TD is a long-established bank with four segments (Canadian personal and commercial banking, US banking, wealth and insurance, wholesale) that a careful generalist can understand, though credit and regulatory risks need care.

b2.evidence: TD has been profitable every year in its modern history, earning C$11,895M in pandemic-hit FY2020 and C$8,842M even in FY2024 after absorbing US AML penalties.

integrity.evidence: TD returns capital rationally (a C$8B FY2026 buyback and 40-50% payout target) and has made AML remediation its top priority, but its October 2024 guilty plea to US Bank Secrecy Act failures showed serious governance and control lapses.

b6.evidence: TD walked away from the First Horizon deal in 2023 and is now simplifying (exiting US retail cards and point-of-sale financing), but its US$1.1B Cowen acquisition in 2023 was a peer-style expansion into investment banking.

roic.evidence: Reported ROE was 15.8% in Q3 2026 but only 8.2% in FY2024 after AML penalties, and it relies on bank leverage of about 15.6x liabilities to equity.

fcf.evidence: Free cash flow is not a meaningful measure for a bank, whose operating cash flow swings with deposits and trading; TD's capacity is better shown by its C$4.20 FY2025 dividend and C$8B FY2026 buyback.

b10.evidence: Reported diluted EPS rose from C$6.43 in FY2020 to C$11.56 in FY2025 (helped by the Schwab gain), but adjusted EPS of C$8.37 in FY2025 shows slower underlying progress and the FY2024 AML penalties destroyed value.

safety.evidence: At about 18x trailing earnings and 2.1x book, the shares trade above analysts' US$115.4 average target, leaving no meaningful margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 16.8 on consensus FY2026 adjusted EPS of C$10.12 and a 2.6% dividend yield is reasonable for a recovering big bank, but no longer cheap versus Canadian peers.

mu5.evidence: TD's 14.3% CET1 ratio and diversified earnings make failure unlikely, but leverage, a Canadian housing downturn and further AML enforcement in the US or by FINTRAC are real ways it could be badly hurt.

reinvest.evidence: TD can reinvest at mid-teens ROE in Canada and wealth, but the US$434B asset cap and capital rules limit how much it can deploy, which is why it is returning about C$15B of excess Schwab capital.

ly2.evidence: TD is a stalwart in a turnaround: a large bank rebuilding after the AML penalties, with a simple story of cost cuts, buybacks and a 16% ROE target by FY2029.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 18 is below the 21% consensus FY2026 adjusted EPS growth, but that growth is a one-off rebound and is above TD's 7-10% medium-term EPS growth target.

runway.evidence: Q3 2026 revenue rose 10.4% to C$16,885M, but long-term growth is tied to the Canadian economy, fee businesses and a US bank capped at US$434B of assets.

ly7.evidence: TD is shrinking its share count (diluted shares 1,652.2M in Q3 2026 vs 1,718.9M a year earlier), but there is no notable insider open-market buying (insiders own about 0.03%).

ly8.evidence: TD is one of Canada's largest companies, worth about US$197B, and is heavily covered by analysts.

fi2.evidence: TD keeps updating digital banking and AI tools and is pushing fee businesses like TD Cowen and wealth, but banking products change slowly.

fi3.evidence: TD does not report R&D, and the payoff from its technology and AI spending is hard to isolate.

fi4.evidence: TD is a leader in Canadian cards, direct investing and insurance and cross-sells to about 17 million Canadian clients and more than 10 million in the US.

longterm.evidence: Under Chun TD is spending about US$550M in FY2026 on AML remediation and investing in risk, controls and technology, while still managing to annual ROE and EPS targets.

gr1.evidence: TD has C$2,111,861M of assets and a market value of about US$197B.

ni10.evidence: TD has reported a profit in each of the last ten fiscal years, with a low of C$8,842M in FY2024.

gr4.evidence: TD and its predecessors have paid dividends without interruption since 1857, and it paid C$4.20 per share in FY2025.

eps10.evidence: Reported diluted EPS rose from C$4.21 in FY2015 to C$11.56 in FY2025, and adjusted EPS from C$4.61 to C$8.37 (+82%), well over one third.

gr6.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 18 is above Graham's limit of about 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 18.2 times P/B of about 2.1 gives about 39, well above Graham's 22.5 ceiling.

th1.evidence: TD's products are similar to those of RBC and the other big banks, with no technology ten times better.

timing.evidence: Strong capital markets and fee income helped TD post record Canadian and Wholesale earnings in Q3 2026, but rate cuts, US tariffs and the US asset cap are headwinds.

th3.evidence: TD grew over more than 150 years in a large national banking market rather than by dominating a small niche first.

team.evidence: TD's management, led by CEO Raymond Chun since February 2025, is experienced, but it is not a founder-led team and oversaw serious US control failures.

th5.evidence: TD has one of the largest branch and digital distribution networks in Canada and a long branch network along the US East Coast.

durable.evidence: Canada's tightly regulated five-bank structure and TD's scale make its Canadian position very likely to hold for 10-20 years, despite fintech challengers.

th7.evidence: TD competes in well-understood markets and has no secret opportunity others fail to see.

trend.evidence: TD aims to scale AI internally, but it is a user rather than a leading beneficiary of a platform shift.

dr1.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 adjusted EPS rose to C$7.59 from C$6.19, Q3 beat consensus (C$2.77 vs C$2.47), and consensus FY2026 adjusted EPS of C$10.12 implies 21% growth.

dr2.evidence: Further cost savings, a new C$6-7B buyback program and progress on AML remediation could lift results, but much of this was laid out at the 2025 Investor Day and is already expected.

dr4.evidence: A steeper yield curve and stable credit help, but Bank of Canada rate cuts and tariff pressure on the Canadian economy work against it.

dr6.evidence: Q4 FY2026 results in early December 2026, a likely dividend increase, the planned new C$6-7B buyback and any easing of the US asset cap are identifiable catalysts.

dr7.evidence: As a leveraged, rate-sensitive bank with unresolved AML regulatory risk and a price above analysts' average target, TD suits a core holding rather than a large concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is not meaningful for a bank; its 30.3% FY2025 net margin was inflated by the Schwab gain and was 26.2% in nine-month FY2026.

fcfyield.evidence: Bank free cash flow is not meaningful; the earnings yield of about 5.5% on trailing reported EPS is a better gauge.

gb2.evidence: Enterprise value is not a meaningful measure for a bank whose deposits and debt are operating items.

pa2.evidence: TD's US AML crisis, asset cap and US$3.088B penalties were a fixable setback that is now largely priced back in, with Q3 2026 reported net income of C$4,615M and ROE back at 15.8%.

pa4.evidence: With a 14.3% CET1 ratio, diversified earnings and its systemic importance in Canada, the chance of permanent loss on TD is low.

wo1.evidence: TD is a bank, not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or genomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Banking costs do not fall quickly with volume; TD is cutting costs through restructuring rather than scale-driven cost declines.

wo3.evidence: TD does not combine several of ARK's innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: TD's addressable market grows with the economy and savings, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: TD's earnings depend heavily on interest rates, credit conditions, capital markets and US regulators.

ns1.evidence: TD keeps its scale savings as margins rather than passing them to customers through lower fees or better rates.

ns4.evidence: TD should be stronger once AML remediation is done and the asset cap lifted, but its long-run position is not clearly stronger than before the scandal.

va2.evidence: Safe savings, mortgages, insurance and business credit solve large real needs, but many banks solve them equally well.

tn1.evidence: TD is a traditional bank adopting AI, not a company built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees TD as a big Canadian bank repairing its US business, which is what it is; there is no hidden transformation story.

tn3.evidence: TD is a US$197B large-cap Canadian bank, outside small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups.

tn4.evidence: Revenue grew in four of the last five fiscal years (to C$67,777M in FY2025) and TD is profitable, but as a bank it carries far more liabilities than cash, a structural reason for the miss.

tn5.evidence: Quarterly free cash flow and cash-versus-debt are not meaningful for a bank whose cash flows swing with deposits and trading.

tn6.evidence: Nine-month FY2026 revenue fell 5.8% to C$49,267M against a base that included the Schwab gain; Q3 2026 revenue rose 10.4%, but consensus implies about 3% growth for FY2026 excluding that gain.

tn7.evidence: Underlying revenue growth in the single digits plus a non-meaningful free-cash-flow margin falls well short of 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue rose 18.4% to C$67,777M while non-interest expenses fell 5.5% to C$33,539M (FY2024 included the AML provision).

tn9.evidence: TD trips the revenue-growth kill (nine-month FY2026 revenue down 5.8%) and, as a bank, its liabilities far exceed its cash.

tn10.evidence: TD remains under US AML consent orders and plea agreements with a US$434B asset cap and a Suspicious Activity Report lookback running to 2027, and FINTRAC's review of its Canadian AML program may bring further action.

tn11.evidence: TD provides banking, wealth, insurance and capital markets services that help households and businesses save, borrow, invest and protect themselves, and charges interest spreads, fees and premiums; clients choose it for convenience, scale and breadth.

tn13.evidence: Total about 60: cash vs debt 5, revenue growth 0, operating margin 10, short interest 10, institutional ownership 5, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 0, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue dipped in FY2021 (C$42,693M vs C$43,646M), net margin swung from 27.3% to 15.5% (FY2024) and back, and bank free cash flow is not consistently positive.

tn15.evidence: As a bank, TD's total liabilities of C$1,984,846M are about 15.6x its C$127,015M of equity (July 31, 2026), far above the 4x test.

tn18.evidence: Chun has been CEO only since February 2025 and is not a founder; his early results are good but there is no notable open-market share buying.

tn20.evidence: TD beat consensus in Q3 2026 (adjusted EPS C$2.77 vs C$2.47) and posted record adjusted profit in Q1 2026, but its record over the AML years was uneven.

tn21.evidence: There is no accounting fraud or auditor change, but TD's criminal guilty plea over US AML failures in October 2024 is a serious governance red flag.

tn22.evidence: TD has large real revenue (C$67,777M in FY2025), strong profits and is buying back shares rather than issuing them.

tn24.evidence: At about 17x forward earnings with a 2.6% yield the price implies mid-to-high single-digit growth, below the current 21% EPS rebound but close to TD's 7-10% medium-term target.

tn25.evidence: Nash's free-cash-flow DCF cannot be applied meaningfully to a bank, whose reported free cash flow is driven by balance-sheet flows.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 16.8 against 21% expected FY2026 EPS growth gives a PEG of about 0.8, but on next-year EPS growth of about 11% (C$11.20) the PEG is about 1.4, at a premium to some Canadian bank peers.
